meta.title: Who really said "An idea, like a ghost, must be spoken to a little before it will explain itself"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Charles Dickens wrote it in Dombey and Son (1846–48) — but in the plural. The familiar singular wording comes from an 1862 quotation compiler.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'An idea, like a ghost, must be spoken to a little before it will explain itself'?
meta.ogDescription: Right author, wrong words. Dickens wrote "Ideas, like ghosts...they will explain themselves" in Dombey and Son. The singular version dates from 1862.

answer.label: Charles Dickens — but not in these words
answer.sourceLine: Dickens wrote the line in chapter 12 of Dombey and Son (serialised 1846–48), but in the plural and with a parenthesis: “Ideas, like ghosts (according to the common notion of ghosts), must be spoken to a little before they will explain themselves.” The tidy singular version quoted today was introduced by a Victorian quotation compiler in 1862 and has circulated ever since.
answer.confidenceText: Genuinely Dickens in substance — but this is not the sentence he wrote.

source.excerpt: Unless young Toots had some idea on the subject, to the expression of which he was wholly unequal. Ideas, like ghosts (according to the common notion of ghosts), must be spoken to a little before they will explain themselves; and Toots had long left off asking any questions of his own mind.
trail: The sentence is in Dickens: chapter 12 of Dombey and Son (1848) at Wikisource ↗ reads “Ideas, like ghosts (according to the common notion of ghosts), must be spoken to a little before they will explain themselves” — plural, in a paragraph about Mr Toots.

Quote Investigator ↗ credits Dickens with the figure of speech and dates the altered singular version to Henry Southgate’s 1862 compilation, tracking its reappearance in 1867, 1872 and 1916 reference works.
Southgate’s book is not a ghost either: the 1862 volume is digitised in full at the Internet Archive ↗.
Publication dates confirmed against the novel’s publication history ↗: monthly parts from 1 October 1846 to 1 April 1848, one volume from Bradbury & Evans on 12 April 1848.
source.excerptNote: Dickens’s wording, verbatim from the 1848 text. The version that circulates today drops the plural, drops the parenthesis, and drops Toots — without whom the sentence is no longer a joke.

source.rightsNote: Dombey and Son was published in London between October 1846 and April 1848, and Henry Southgate’s Many Thoughts of Many Minds in 1862 — both far earlier than 1931, so the original sentence and the altered singular version are alike in the public domain in the United States. Dickens wrote in English, so no translation copyright arises.

author.bio: Charles Dickens (7 February 1812 – 9 June 1870) was an English writer and journalist, and the defining novelist of the Victorian era. Dombey and Son — published in nineteen monthly parts from October 1846 to April 1848 and in one volume that April — came at the height of his powers, and its portrait of the wealthy, emotionally frozen Mr Dombey is one of his sharpest studies of pride. The ghost simile belongs to a comic aside about Mr Toots, a good-natured young man whose head Dickens describes as a leaden casket that never quite gives up its contents.

cite.sourceCitation: Charles Dickens, Dealings with the Firm of Dombey and Son, Wholesale, Retail, and for Exportation (London: Bradbury & Evans, 1848), chap. 12, “Paul’s Education.” The popular singular wording is earliest documented in Henry Southgate, comp., Many Thoughts of Many Minds (London: Griffin, Bohn, 1862).

misattribution.heading: Right author, rewritten words
misattribution.intro: Nobody stole this line from Dickens — but almost nobody quotes it as he wrote it. Two changes separate the popular version from the novel: the plural became singular, and Dickens’s parenthesis vanished.

items.who: Henry Southgate, Many Thoughts of Many Minds (1862)
items.why: The earliest instance of the singular form documented by Quote Investigator ↗, filed under the topic heading “Evoking an Idea”: “An idea, like a ghost (according to the common notion of ghosts), must be spoken to a little before it will explain itself.”

items.who: Frank J. Wilstach, A Dictionary of Similes (1916)
items.why: Reprinted Southgate’s singular wording rather than the novel’s, carrying the alteration into the twentieth century’s standard reference on similes — one of several such reprintings listed by Quote Investigator ↗.

Goodreads, AZQuotes and their imitators print the fourteen-word singular version with the parenthesis removed and no work named at all ↗ — which is why the line is so often quoted as a free-floating maxim about creativity rather than as a joke about a slow-witted schoolboy.

misattribution.truthLine: What Dickens actually printed, in chapter 12 of Dombey and Son ↗: “Ideas, like ghosts (according to the common notion of ghosts), must be spoken to a little before they will explain themselves.”

context.heading: A line about unexamined ideas, itself never examined
lead: Dickens is not writing an aphorism here — he is making a joke at the expense of Mr Toots, a wealthy, amiable young man at Doctor Blimber’s school whose brain Dickens likens to a leaden casket giving off a mist that never takes shape. Toots feels something about little Paul Dombey that he cannot say, and the narrator explains why: ideas, like ghosts, have to be questioned before they will account for themselves, “and Toots had long left off asking any questions of his own mind.”

Lifted out of that paragraph the sentence became a maxim about creativity, and it has been quoted that way for more than a century and a half — in the singular, with Dickens’s hedging parenthesis quietly removed. The irony is hard to miss: a line about how ideas must be interrogated before they explain themselves has itself gone uninterrogated by nearly everyone who has repeated it.
detailsBody: Dickens, 1846–48. “Ideas, like ghosts (according to the common notion of ghosts), must be spoken to a little before they will explain themselves” — plural subject, plural verb, parenthesis intact.
Southgate, 1862. Recast into the singular for a quotation treasury and filed under the topic heading “Evoking an Idea,” per Quote Investigator ↗.
Today. The parenthesis has gone too, leaving the fourteen-word version that circulates on quote sites with no work named at all.
context.pull: Ideas, like ghosts, have to be spoken to — and so, it turns out, do quotations.

sourcesVerified.claim: Quote Investigator credits Dickens with the ideas/ghosts simile in Dombey and Son, gives the original plural wording, and dates the singular rewrite to Henry Southgate's 1862 Many Thoughts of Many Minds (topic heading 'Evoking an Idea'), with later instances in 1867 The Lady's Own Paper, 1872 A Cyclopedia of the Best Thoughts of Charles Dickens, and 1916 Wilstach's A Dictionary of Similes.

Chapter 12 of Dombey and Son ('Paul's Education') contains verbatim: 'Unless young Toots had some idea on the subject, to the expression of which he was wholly unequal. Ideas, like ghosts (according to the common notion of ghosts), must be spoken to a little before they will explain themselves; and Toots had long left off asking any questions of his own mind.'
Independent second transcription confirming the same sentence in chapter 12, titled 'Paul's Education'.
Dombey and Son was serialised in nineteen monthly parts from 1 October 1846 to 1 April 1848 and published in one volume on 12 April 1848 by Bradbury & Evans.
